title: Paving, edging and soft-landscape installation
audience: Landscape installers and crew leaders who prepare bases, lay pavers and edging, and install soft-landscape edging and borders.
learningOutcomes: Prepare a compacted base for paving with the right depth, falls and drainage for the surface and the load.
Lay pavers and install edge restraints so that the surface is level, stable and free from trip hazards.
Cut and handle pavers and stone with controls for silica dust, manual handling and noise.
Price paving and edging work by area, base depth, edge length, cutting, waste and access, rather than by a flat rate.

instruction.heading: Why the base decides the result
instruction.body: Most paving failures begin below the surface. A base that is too thin, poorly compacted or laid on soft ground will settle, rock and crack under foot and vehicle traffic. Good paving is a sequence of decisions: how deep the base must be for the expected load, how the surface will drain, how the edges will be held, and how the finished surface will feel underfoot. Paving is a higher-value service because it takes skill and materials, and because clients judge the result by its levels and finish. Spend the time on the base, check it before the bedding goes down, and record its depth and compaction.

instruction.heading: Preparing the base and drainage
instruction.body: Excavate to the depth for the planned base, allowing for the bedding layer and the paver thickness, and mark the finished levels with stakes or a string line. Remove soft and organic material, and check for services before any digging. Compact the subgrade in layers, using a plate compactor where it is suitable, and check the compaction at each stage. Build the base from a granular material in layers, compacting each layer, and check the depth as you go. Set falls so that water runs away from buildings and does not pool on the surface. The fall needed depends on the surface and the site, and the client's drainage path must be checked on the plan. A plate compactor is noisy and vibrates the body. The Safe Work Australia noise code (October 2018) sets the noise exposure standard at 85 dB(A) averaged over an 8-hour day, with a peak limit of 140 dB(C). It treats hearing protection as the last line of defence, after the noise source has been controlled, so use it and rotate workers where the procedure requires it.

instruction.heading: Laying pavers and edge restraints
instruction.body: Lay a thin bedding layer, screed it level to the stakes, and lay the pavers from a fixed starting line. Set each paver firmly, check its level with a straightedge, and keep the joints even. Fill the joints with the approved material, sweep it in, and compact the surface. Install edge restraints before the final pavers are placed, so that the edges do not move under load. Soft-landscape edging, such as timber or metal edging for garden beds, is set to a line and fixed firmly so that it does not heave or sink. Check that the finished surface has no trip hazard, such as a lip between two pavers, and that the falls are right. Re-check the levels after the first rain or wetting, and record any settlement.

instruction.heading: Cutting, handling and dust control
instruction.body: Pavers and stone are heavy, and cutting them creates both dust and noise. Plan the cutting before the work starts, so that most cuts are made in one controlled place rather than in the middle of the laying. For masonry and concrete, use wet cutting or local exhaust ventilation. Safe Work Australia's silica guidance (July 2024) treats wet processing and local exhaust ventilation as engineering controls, and gives the workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica as 0.05 mg/m3, averaged over an 8-hour day. Wet cutting or exhaust does not by itself remove the need for a risk assessment, and where practicable the cutting should be done outdoors in a designated area away from other people. Where dry cutting is unavoidable, use an extraction system approved by the business and a respirator selected for the hazard. Keep bystanders and neighbours away from the cutting zone, and clean up slurry and waste with methods that do not raise dust. Lift pavers with a trolley or a clamp rather than carrying them by hand. Safe Work Australia's manual tasks guidance says a business must assess manual tasks and manage their risks as far as reasonably practicable (no date shown). Keep walkways clear of cut offcuts and slurry, which are slip and trip hazards.

instruction.heading: Pricing and quoting paving work
instruction.body: Paving is a higher-value service because it needs skill, materials and time to prepare the base. Price it from the components: the area, the base depth and material, the bedding and jointing material, the edge restraints, the cutting and waste, the access and the time for levels and checks. Quote soft-landscape edging separately from the paving, because its length and fixing method differ. Give the client a clear quote showing these components, and explain what is included in the base depth. Do not promise a surface that will never settle, because ground conditions and drainage affect the result. Record the quote and the client's approval before materials are ordered, and use the business's pricing method and approval steps.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the base, the levels, the cutting controls and the quote. A competent installer can show the base depth and compaction record, explain how falls were set, identify a trip hazard, describe the dust controls used and explain how the quote was built. Escalate any soft ground or unexpected service found during excavation, any level or fall that cannot be achieved on the approved plan, any cutting that cannot be controlled, and any request to change the surface or the drainage path after approval.

procedure: Confirm the approved scope, levels, falls and drainage path on the plan, and check the services locations.
Excavate to the planned depth, remove soft material and set the finished levels with stakes and a string line.
Compact the subgrade and build the base in layers, checking compaction and depth at each layer.
Lay the bedding layer, screed it to the stakes and check the fall with a level or a straightedge.
Install edge restraints before the final pavers are placed, and set soft-landscape edging to a line.
Lay the pavers from a fixed starting line, check each level and fill the joints with the approved material.
Cut pavers with wet cutting or dust controls, keep the work area clear, and clean up slurry and waste.
Record the base depth, the compaction checks, the falls, the materials used and the client sign-off, and re-check after the first wetting.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a paved patio of 20 square metres with one edge against a garden bed and a step down to the lawn. The base has been dug and some soft soil remains in one corner.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before laying the bedding?
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove the soft soil from the corner and replace it with compacted base material, compacting in layers. Check the depth and the fall against the plan, and confirm the step level with the client. Install the edge restraint on the bed side before laying the pavers. Record the compaction and depth at the corner, because a soft spot there will show as a dip in the finished surface.

workedExamples.situation: A crew needs to cut 40 pavers to fit around a tree root flare and a drain grate. The cutting will produce a lot of dust.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you control dust and exposure?
workedExamples.reasoning: Use wet cutting or a dust-extraction method approved by the business, and keep the cutting area away from people and from the neighbour's property. Wear a respirator selected for the hazard, eye protection and hearing protection. Do not dry-sweep the dust. Clean up the slurry and waste under the business's procedure, and record the controls used. The workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica is 0.05 mg/m3, averaged over 8 hours, so check the controls against that figure.

equipmentAndPpe: Plate compactor, inspected before use, with hearing protection
Wet cutting saw or dust-extraction equipment approved by the business
Respirator suitable for silica dust, fit-tested where the business's procedure requires
Straightedge, level, stakes and string line
Manual-handling aids such as a paver trolley or lifting clamp

commonErrors.error: Laying the bedding on a base that has not been compacted in layers.
commonErrors.prevention: Build and compact the base in layers, and check depth and compaction before bedding.

commonErrors.error: Dry-cutting pavers and creating silica dust that spreads to neighbours and workers.
commonErrors.prevention: Use wet cutting or the approved extraction, and clean up with methods that do not raise dust.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a lip between pavers or an uneven edge that becomes a trip hazard.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each paver with a straightedge and correct it before the joints are filled.

commonErrors.error: Pricing paving at a flat rate per square metre without the base depth, cutting or access.
commonErrors.prevention: Price base depth, cutting, edge length, waste and access separately.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Crystalline silica: the workplace exposure standard for respirable crystalline silica is 0.05 mg/m3 as an 8-hour time-weighted average (guidance dated July 2024). Wet processing or local exhaust ventilation are the engineering controls named for cutting masonry and concrete. Confirm the current standard before stating any limit to a worker.
Noise: the noise exposure standard is 85 dB(A) averaged over 8 hours, with a peak of 140 dB(C) (code dated October 2018). Hearing protection is the last line of defence.
Manual handling: a business must assess manual tasks and manage their risks as far as reasonably practicable (no date shown). No weight limit is set in this lesson.
Structures, retaining elements and work that changes drainage or affects a neighbour may need approval or a licence holder. See the scope lesson for the boundary.

qualityStandard: The base depth, compaction checks and falls match the approved plan and are recorded.
The finished surface has no trip hazard, and levels are checked with a straightedge.
Edge restraints are installed before the final pavers and are secure.
Dust and slurry have been controlled and cleaned up under the business's procedure.
documentationEvidence: Base record with the depth, the material, the compaction checks and the date.
Level and fall check record for the finished surface.
Silica and dust control record for any cutting, with the equipment used.
Client sign-off and a re-check record after the first wetting.
summary: Paving is only as good as its base. Compact in layers and check depth and falls.
Install edge restraints before the final pavers, and check every level.
Control silica dust with wet cutting or approved extraction.
Price the base depth, cutting, edging, waste and access, not a flat rate.

knowledgeChecks.question: A soft spot is found in the corner of an excavated paving base. What is the correct action?
options: Lay the bedding over it and let the pavers settle, since the sand will fill any gap in the base
Ignore it, because the pavers will hide any dip once they are laid and sealed in the joints
Remove the soft material, replace it with compacted base in layers, and check the depth and fall.

knowledgeChecks.question: Pavers must be cut on site and the work will create dust. Which control is most appropriate?
options: Use wet cutting or approved extraction, with respirator and eye protection, and clean up without raising dust.
Dry-cut and sweep the dust into the garden bed, since the bed is close and the dust will settle there
Cut them quickly with the neighbour's door closed, so the dust stays on the site and not inside

knowledgeChecks.question: How should paving be priced?
options: A single flat rate per square metre for every job, to keep the quote simple
By base depth, cutting, edge length, waste and access, each priced separately.
By the number of hours the crew expects to be on the job, including drive time
